newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Perry says Stealth fighters to stay in Kuwait.
newsitem.headline: Perry says Stealth fighters to stay in Kuwait.

text.p: The United States has decided not to remove eight F-117A "Stealth" fighters from Kuwait and will keep them there as a message to Iraq's president Saddam Hussein not to invade Kuwait again, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Friday.
"We were considering redeploying them but we have decided to leave them here for an indefinite period of time," Perry said during a visit to the Gulf state.

The jets were rushed to Kuwait in September in a confrontation between the United States and Iraq over attacks by Saddam's military forces against Kurds in northern Iraq. They had been expected to return to the United states early next month.

But Perry told a group of U.S. soldiers after talks with Kuwait's Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Sabah and Defence Minister Sheikh Salem al-Sabah that he had informed the Kuwaiti officials that the radar-avoiding jets would stay as part of "a message to Saddam Hussein don't even think about coming back."
A U.S.-led military coalition defeated Saddam's forces in the 1991 Gulf War and drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

Perry, mid-way through a globe-circling trip that will also take him to Qatar and Saudi Arabia on Friday, said that the United States would remove 4,200 American troops from Kuwait by Christmas but would maintain 1,800 Marines aboard ships off-shore to be ready after U.S. troops leave Kuwait next month.
Three thousand of those U.S. army troops were sent to Kuwait in September along with the "Stealth" fighters.
"I don't think you can ever take your eyes off Saddam Hussein," Perry said on Thursday.
He also said U.S. and Saudi Arabian intelligence efforts averted possible new "terrorist" attacks in the kingdom and the American military remains on high alert there.
He told reporters flying with him that there had been a number of arrests to prevent possible attacks in the kingdom.
A total of 24 U.S. soldiers were killed in two bomb attacks in Saudi Arabia in November, 1995, and in June of this year. Investigations continue into those incidents.
He said anonymous threats were received weekly by the Saudis or the U.S. military, and while many may be harassment or hoaxes, they were taken seriously. He declined to give details.

"These are cases where I cannot discuss details," Perry said of the averted attacks. "They were based on intelligence information we or the Saudis had. Based on that information, either they or we took action and it, in our judgement, averted what would have been some sort of a terrorist attempted action."
Perry was asked about published reports from Dubai this week that a radical Islamic group threatened to attack U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia unless jailed Moslem militants were freed.
The statement from the Movement for Islamic Change was the second since a June 25 truck bomb of a U.S. military housing complex in eastern Saudi Arabia in which 19 U.S. troops died.
Since that attack, the U.S. military has moved nearly 4,000 of its air force personnel to a remote Prince Sultan Air Base in the desert and is improving security for troops in Riyadh.

"Both we and the Saudis have a very intensive intelligence effort to uncover hard information about what's going on. That information also supports the view that we should remain on a high alert," Perry said.

The Saudi government executed four Saudi citizens in the first bombing and Saudi authorities and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation are cooperating in an inquiry into the June 25 blast at the military housing facility at Dhahran.
No culprits have been announced in the second bombing attack although published reports said the Saudis arrested as many as 40 people in connection with the investigation.
